strengths: Slides 1, 6, and 7 sustain a brief-specific history-detective premise through the tax paper, map, letter, and food basket rather than applying a generic playful skin.

Slide 5 uses four warm, nonviolent character illustrations to make unequal experiences visible; the explicit label that these are illustrative viewpoints rather than real biographies protects historical integrity.
The sequence from location to causes, duration, viewpoints, objects, outcomes, and quiz is coherent and instructional.
Slides 3 and 7 avoid a simplistic heroes-versus-villains account and clearly state that ending the conflict did not end slavery or make life fair.
The cream, red, mustard, teal, and pink palette is colorful without becoming chaotic, and most text remains projection-readable.

issues.evidence: Generation/layout defect: the intended label beneath the Rio Grande do Sul panel wraps into one letter per line as “story center” and runs off the bottom edge. This fails the unclipped-content hard check.
issues.fix: Replace it with a short horizontal label inside the card, reduce the map graphic slightly, and verify the complete slide against a safe-area grid.

issues.evidence: The three map graphics are abstract blobs with no recognizable coastline, neighboring geography, or clear state outline. They communicate nesting through arrows but do not actually help children locate Rio Grande do Sul.
issues.fix: Use simplified but recognizable outlines of South America and Brazil, then highlight southern Brazil and Rio Grande do Sul with consistent zoom boxes.

issues.evidence: The timeline contains only a beginning, an ending, and a generic “long middle.” It shows duration but no event, shift, or relationship that explains why the war lasted ten years.
issues.fix: Add two or three carefully sourced, nonviolent milestones using simple icons, while retaining the child-friendly comparison with years in primary school.

issues.evidence: The answers are already displayed in the “Check” strip directly below the questions, weakening the quiz task in the static rendered slide.
issues.fix: Place the answer key on a following slide or use a clearly functioning reveal state.

issues.evidence: The causal claims are followed only by an underlined institution name rather than a source title, URL, or other verifiable reference.
issues.fix: Add a compact source line with the specific archive page or publication used, and connect it to the claims on this slide.

A.signatureMoment: Slide 7 reconnects the recurring objects with a red cord and pairs that image with a clear changed-versus-unchanged synthesis; it is the deck’s strongest union of premise, imagery, and historical meaning.

strengths: Large typography and pastel category colors create an immediately legible visual system where content remains inside the frame.
Slide 3 groups four causes more clearly than a conventional bullet list.
Slide 6 directly pairs each everyday object with a question children can discuss.
The deck avoids violent battle imagery and the visible historical claims are broadly consistent with the requested topic.

issues.evidence: Generation defect: the object composite is displayed over a baked-in transparency checkerboard inside the image panel, making the opening look like an unfinished asset preview.
issues.fix: Regenerate or properly export the object image with a clean opaque background and crop it to use the large panel intentionally.

issues.evidence: The entire rightmost location card is outside the frame; only fragments such as “Rio G...” and “The c...” are visible. The required destination of the map sequence is therefore unreadable.
issues.fix: Reflow the three cards within the slide width, reduce card and type size, and test at the final presentation dimensions.

issues.evidence: Both lower cause cards continue below the slide edge, cutting off their explanatory text.
issues.fix: Reduce heading and body size or shorten the copy so all four cards fit with a visible bottom margin.

issues.evidence: The central 1835–1845 milestone is clipped at the bottom, leaving the timeline’s middle explanation incomplete.
issues.fix: Move the timeline upward and reserve a fixed lower safe area for the middle milestone and its description.

issues.evidence: The lower two viewpoint cards are cut off, so Luzia and Davi cannot be read. The slide also substitutes generic line icons for the illustrated characters explicitly requested.
issues.fix: Use four complete illustrated character portraits in a compact row or two-by-two layout, with one short sentence per viewpoint.

issues.evidence: Selection defect: the required everyday objects are represented only by generic interface-style icons. They identify nouns but provide none of the tactile historical-clue quality seen in the opening premise.
issues.fix: Replace the icons with simple illustrated reconstructions of the tax paper, folded map, letter, and food basket.

issues.evidence: The right-hand panel reaches the bottom edge and its final explanation is visibly crowded or clipped, preventing reliable reading of the slavery outcome.
issues.fix: Shorten the text and add a substantial bottom margin; preserve the strong two-column changed-versus-unchanged comparison.

issues.evidence: Only “Question 1 of 3” is visible, no answer is rendered, and the top of another blue element is cut off at the bottom. As delivered, the required quiz is incomplete unless unverified interactivity is assumed.
issues.fix: Render all three questions and answers as complete slides or provide visibly functional reveal states, with every element inside the frame.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 6 has the clearest child-facing discussion structure, but its generic icons and four repeated cards keep it from becoming a memorable substantive visual.

result.reason: A is the deck I would give the user after correcting slide 2. It more fully delivers the requested illustrated characters, everyday objects, simple map, timeline, nonviolent storytelling, and quiz, and its object-based detective premise continues through the ending. The preference does not reverse when the comparison order is considered. Both decks use eight slides and satisfy the broad colorful-palette request, but neither is ready as rendered: A has one hard clipping failure, while B has pervasive clipping plus a missing illustrated-character treatment. The single most important improvement for B is to rebuild every slide on a fixed safe-area grid so the complete content fits; that would remove its dominant failure before decorative refinement. Route identity is unavailable, but the greater visible complexity in A earns itself on slides 5–7 because it improves explanation rather than merely adding ornament. A exceeds competent default quality in concept and selected visuals, though not yet in final craft.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: Replace slide 2 with a geographically recognizable nested map, turn slide 4 into a sourced visual sequence with meaningful middle milestones, eliminate the overflow, and move the slide 8 answers into a genuine reveal. That would let the strong detective-object premise remain convincing through both the informational middle and the ending.
